The package never renders or sends mail. Each flow that needs one emits a typed `AuthMailEvent` to your `Mailer`, and your code turns it into a message in your own templates and language.

## Why `send` must enqueue

Each flow calls `send` and answers without awaiting the promise it returns, so a delivery that is slow, or never settles, neither delays nor hangs a response. In most flows the call itself is on the response path, though: whatever your `send` does before it returns its promise counts toward the response time, and a door that mails on one branch only (a lock notice, a password-changed mail) would answer slower on that branch. A `send` that rendered the template, or opened an SMTP connection, before returning would make the two branches take different times and give the answer back. So `Mailer.send` must store a job and return; a worker builds the template and sends it. Sign-up hands both of its templates (`account-exists` for a taken address, `verify-email` for a new one) over from a background task, after a store call: the answer does not wait for that call, so with a store on the network `send` runs after the answer, and an end-to-end test that reads the mail right after sign-up must wait for it.

Delivery from the library is at most once. Each mail is handed to `send` once; a `send` that throws or rejects does not fail the flow, the error goes to the configured `logger` as `Mailer failed` with the event type and user id, and the mail is not retried. Retries are the job of your queue. Make sure your queue is up, and give `createAuth` a logger.

## Keeping sends alive, and bounding them

Enqueueing narrows the window in which a mail can be lost, but does not close it on its own. The library does not await the enqueue, so if the process exits, or a serverless runtime freezes the instance once the response is sent, before the queue write settles, that mail is lost. Every mail, every lock notice and a reset job run without `enqueue` go through one background runner, configured by the `background` option of `createAuth`:

- **On a runtime that freezes after the response** (Vercel, Cloudflare Workers and similar), pass its `waitUntil`. The runner hands it each task's promise as the task starts; the promise never rejects. On Workers the function belongs to the request (`ctx.waitUntil`), so build `auth` per request there, or keep the request's `ctx` somewhere your `waitUntil` can reach it.
- **On a long-lived Node process**, call `await auth.flush()` during graceful shutdown, after the server stops taking requests and before you close the database and Redis connections. It resolves once no task is left that has neither settled nor timed out, tasks started while it waits included, and never rejects. Pass `{ timeout }` to bound the wait: after that long it logs `Background flush stopped waiting`, with the labels of the tasks still running, and resolves, so a send that never settles cannot hold shutdown forever. With `@noctcore/auth-nestjs`, `AuthModule` does this for you on shutdown, bounded to 10 seconds by default.
- **`background.timeout`** (a `Duration`) stops waiting on a task that is still running after it: the task is logged as `Background task timed out: <label>` and counted, and `flush` and `waitUntil` stop waiting for it. JavaScript cannot cancel a promise, so the send itself keeps running and keeps whatever it holds in memory until it settles. Give your enqueue its own timeout too.
- **`background.maxPending`** bounds memory while a mailer hangs instead of failing: while that many tasks are still running, timed out or not, a new task is not started. It is logged as `Background task dropped: <label>`, with the user id when there is one, and counted. A dropped mail is not retried, like any other failed send. Each mail is one capped task (`mail <type>`, such as `mail lockout`), and a sign-up's verification mail is one capped task that issues the code and hands the mail over (`verification mail`). Work that writes an audit row runs outside the cap and is never dropped: the `register.created`, `account.locked` and `account.locked_permanently` rows (tasks labelled `audit <type>`), the taken-address half of a sign-up (`existing address notice`: the owner lookup and the `register.existing` row) and a reset job run without `enqueue` (`password reset job`: the lookup, the mail limit and the `password.reset_request_ignored` row). Only the mail these start is capped. So under `maxPending` you can lose a mail, and with a dropped verification mail its `email.verification_sent` row (a dropped mail was not sent), but no other audit row. Uncapped tasks still count for `timeout`, `waitUntil` and `flush`, but take no slots: a hung audit sink, or a user store that hangs during those two lookups, grows memory the way it did before `maxPending`, so keep the sink's and the store's own calls bounded. While the cap is full, the drop log names the mail that was dropped, `mail account-exists` for a taken address and `verification mail` for a new one, so the logs of the two sign-up branches differ; the answer to the client does not.

### A dropped or failed mail still spends the budget

The per-account mail limits are spent before the mail is handed to the background runner: `password-reset-mail`, `email-verification-request` and `email-change-request` (3 per `'1h'` by default) all work this way. A mail that is then dropped under `maxPending`, or that the mailer fails to send, never reaches the user but still counts against their budget. While the cap is full or the mailer is failing, up to 3 requests an hour can be used up with no mail sent, and the account cannot ask again until the window ends. The client gets the same answer either way, so neither side sees it. Nothing is refunded and nothing is retried.

Watch the signal on your side: the `Background task dropped: <label>` and `Mailer failed` log lines (pass a `logger`), and the `dropped` outcome of the `auth_background_task` metric. A steady count means the cap is too low or the mailer is unhealthy, and users are being locked out of reset, verification or email change for the rest of the hour.

Timeouts and drops are counted on your `metrics` as `auth_background_task`, with the labels `task` (such as `mail verify-email`) and `outcome` (`timed_out` or `dropped`). None of the three is set by default: tasks run detached, with no timeout and no cap. Drops, timeouts and failures are logged through your `logger`, and the default logger is silent, so pass a `logger` (and `metrics`) or you will not see them.

## The events

| `type` | Sent when | Fields beyond `to`, `userId` and `dedupeKey` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `verify-email` | a new account registers, or a signed-in user asks for another | `code` (code mode) or `url` (link mode), `expiresAt` |
| `password-reset` | a reset is requested for a known address, link mode | `url`, `expiresAt` |
| `password-reset-code` | the same, code mode | `code`, `expiresAt` |
| `password-changed` | a password was changed or reset | `at` |
| `account-exists` | someone registered with an address that already has an account | none |
| `lockout` | failed sign-ins locked the account | `until`, `permanent` (only with the opt-in permanent tier: the lock holds until an admin clears it and `until` is only its stored far-future expiry, so say that instead of printing the date) |
| `email-change-confirm` | an email change was requested for a free address; sent to the new address | `code` (code mode) or `url` (link mode), `expiresAt` |
| `email-change-in-use` | an email change named an address that already has an account; sent to that address, `userId` is its account | none |
| `email-changed` | an email change was confirmed; sent to the address it replaced | `newEmail`, `at`, `revertUrl`, `revertExpiresAt` |
| `email-change-reverted` | a revert link restored the address; every session ended and the password must be reset | `at` |
| `two-factor-enabled` | the two-factor plugin: a second factor was turned on | `at` |
| `two-factor-disabled` | the two-factor plugin: the second factor was turned off | `at` |
| `recovery-code-used` | the two-factor plugin: a recovery code was spent | `remaining` (null when the count could not be read), `at` |
| `invitation` | the invitations plugin: an invitation to a scope; no `userId`, since the address may have no account | `scope`, `inviterId`, `url`, `expiresAt` |

`account-exists` is the other half of the uniform registration answer: the caller sees "check your email" either way, and only the owner of the address learns the account exists. `lockout` tells the owner someone is guessing their password. `email-change-in-use` plays the same part for an email change, and `email-changed` is the owner's way back when the change was not theirs ([Email change](/auth/build/email-change/)).

`dedupeKey` is a server-minted nonce, unique per event and safe to use as a job id, so a retried enqueue stores one job.

### Where the request came from

Mails to the address an account already holds carry an optional `meta`: `{ ip, userAgent? }`, the client IP (after trust-proxy resolution) and the user agent when your framework passed one. They are `password-reset`, `password-reset-code`, `password-changed`, `lockout`, `account-exists`, `email-changed`, `email-change-reverted`, `two-factor-enabled`, `two-factor-disabled` and `recovery-code-used`. Use it for "asked from this IP" in a reset, lockout or security mail. On `account-exists` it is the IP of whoever tried to sign up with the holder's address. A reset mail takes it from the reset job, so it is there when the job runs on your queue, far from the request. `verify-email` after a sign-up and `email-change-confirm` never carry it: they go to an address the request named itself and nobody has proven yet. `email-change-in-use` and `invitation` never carry it either: they go to someone other than the account the request acted on. A mailer that ignores `meta` keeps working.

`meta` is personal data. If your queue stores the event, it stores the IP and user agent too: keep the retention of the mail queue in line with what your privacy policy says about them.

## A queue interface

The samples use the two calls every job queue has in some form. Map them onto BullMQ, pg-boss, Graphile Worker, SQS or whatever you run.

<Code code={queueTs} lang="ts" title="src/mail/queue.ts" />

## One template per event

A `switch` over `event.type` with a `never` check in the `default` branch: if a release adds an event type, your build fails until it has a template, instead of the mail silently going missing.

<Code code={templatesTs} lang="ts" title="src/mail/templates.ts" />

Codes and links are credentials. Keep them out of logs and analytics, and if your queue stores job data in plain text, give its storage the same care as your session store.

## The mailer

<Code code={mailerTs} lang="ts" title="src/mail/mailer.ts" />

The queue holds the raw `AuthMailEvent`: `send` renders nothing. Your worker takes each event off the queue, runs `handleMailJob` (which renders the template and hands the `OutgoingMail` to your mail provider), and retries on failure as your queue allows. If your queue stores job data as JSON, the event's `Date` fields come back as strings, so revive them before rendering.

## Password reset jobs

A reset request answers the same for every address and does none of the per-account work on the response path. It builds a `PasswordResetJob` (`email`, `ip`, `userAgent` when the request had one, and a `dedupeKey`); the lookup, the per-account mail limit and the mail happen when that job runs, in `auth.jobs.processPasswordReset(job)`.

Without `passwordReset.enqueue` the job runs detached in the same process. That keeps the response time independent of the address but loses the job if the process dies. With `enqueue`, the job goes on your queue and your worker runs it:

<Code code={configTs} lang="ts" title="src/mail/config.ts" />

Spread `mailConfig(queues)` into your `createAuth` config, and register `handlePasswordResetJob` as the handler of the reset queue.

- The job's `dedupeKey` is the same for every request for one address within a minute, so a burst of requests stores one job and sends one mail.
- `processPasswordReset` writes `password.reset_request_ignored` to the audit trail when it sends nothing (unknown address, a hook refused, the per-account limit of 3 mails an hour), so the reason is recorded even though the client was answered long before. When it sends a link or code it writes `password.reset_issued` with the user and `data.kind` (`link` or `code`), after the token is stored and before the mail is handed over. Both rows carry the request's IP and user agent from the job.
- A job queued by an older version has no `userAgent`; it runs the same, and its mail's `meta` holds only the IP.
- The job carries the address in plain text. Treat the reset queue's storage like the mail queue's.
